gancho: Em 1996, cientistas da NASA anunciaram possíveis fósseis de bactérias marcianas num meteorito achado na Antártida, e o presidente Clinton foi à TV. Em 2022, um estudo concluiu que as moléculas dele se formaram sem vida.
explicacao: A pedra, batizada de ALH84001, foi recolhida em 27 de dezembro de 1984 nas colinas Allan, na Antártida, e pesava 1,93 kg. Ela veio de Marte: um impacto a arrancou de lá há cerca de 17 milhões de anos, e ela caiu na Terra há uns 13 mil anos. É de uma época em que Marte talvez tivesse água líquida na superfície. Em agosto de 1996, uma equipe liderada por David McKay, da NASA, anunciou que ela podia conter sinais de vida. No microscópio eletrônico havia estruturas de 20 a 100 nanômetros parecidas com bactérias fossilizadas, menores que qualquer célula conhecida na época. Havia também cristais de magnetita iguais aos que bactérias produzem na Terra. O anúncio virou manchete no mundo todo e levou Bill Clinton a fazer um pronunciamento na televisão. A polêmica veio logo: em 2001, cientistas produziram magnetita parecida sem nenhum ser vivo, e muitos lembraram que forma, sozinha, não prova vida. Em 2022, um estudo concluiu que as moléculas orgânicas da pedra surgiram de reações entre rocha e fluidos quentes no Marte primitivo. Mesmo assim, o caso é visto como um marco no nascimento da astrobiologia.

fontes.trecho: Allan Hills 84001 (ALH84001) is a fragment of a Martian meteorite that was found in the Allan Hills in Antarctica on December 27, 1984 [...] Its mass upon discovery was 1.93 kilograms (4.3 lb). [...] culminating in U.S. president Bill Clinton giving a speech about the potential discovery. [...] the initial paper and the enormous scientific and public attention caused by it are considered turning points in the history of the developing science of astrobiology. [...] The theory holds that ALH84001 was blasted away from the surface of Mars by the impact of a meteor about 17 million years ago, and fell on Earth about 13,000 years ago. [...] ALH84001 is the only meteorite originating from when Mars may have had liquid surface water. [...] On August 6, 1996, a team of researchers led by NASA scientists including lead author David S. McKay announced that the meteorite may contain trace evidence of life from Mars. [...] Under a scanning electron microscope, structures were visible that some scientists interpreted as fossils of bacteria-like lifeforms. The structures found on ALH84001 are 20–100 nanometres in diameter, similar in size to theoretical nanobacteria, but smaller than any cellular life known at the time of their discovery. [...] making headlines around the world, and even prompting President of the United States Bill Clinton to make a formal televised announcement to mark the event. [...] indistinguishable from magnetite produced biologically on Earth [...] However, in 2001, scientists were able to explain and produce carbonate globules containing similar magnetite grains through an inorganic process [...] "morphology alone cannot be used unambiguously as a tool for primitive life detection." [...] A later study in January 2022 concluded that ALH84001 did not contain Martian life; the discovered organic molecules were found to be associated with abiotic processes (i.e., "serpentinization and carbonation reactions that occurred during the aqueous alteration of basalt rock by hydrothermal fluids") produced on the very early Mars 4 billion years ago instead.

gancho: Em 1976, um teste das sondas Viking em Marte deu positivo para vida: o solo soltou gás marcado logo após receber nutrientes. A maioria concluiu que era química, mas o autor do teste seguiu defendendo a vida.
explicacao: No experimento Labeled Release, chefiado por Gilbert Levin, uma amostra de solo marciano recebia uma gota de nutrientes marcados com carbono-14, radioativo. Se micróbios comessem a mistura, soltariam gás radioativo. Para surpresa geral, as primeiras injeções deram positivo nas duas sondas: numa, com solo exposto ao Sol; na outra, com solo tirado de baixo de uma pedra. Amostras aquecidas a 160 °C por 3 horas não soltaram gás, como se esperaria se houvesse vida. Mas havia problemas. Na segunda e na terceira injeção não saiu mais gás, o contrário do que fazem bactérias num solo terrestre. E outro instrumento não achou quantidade significativa de matéria orgânica. A explicação mais aceita é química: sem camada de ozônio, a luz ultravioleta cria no solo oxidantes fortes, como superóxidos, que oxidam os nutrientes e se desfazem com o calor. Em 2008, a sonda Phoenix achou perclorato em Marte, sal que destrói orgânicos quando aquecido, o que pode ter mascarado o teste de orgânicos da Viking. Hoje os resultados são vistos como inconclusivos e explicáveis só pela química. Em 2000, Levin ainda sustentava que tinha detectado vida, e em 2012 assinou um artigo que sugeria vida microbiana atual em Marte.

fontes.trecho: In 1976, two identical Viking program landers each carried four types of biological experiments to the surface of Mars. [...] The GCMS measured no significant amount of organic molecules in the Martian soil. [...] Experiments conducted in 2008 by the Phoenix lander discovered the presence of perchlorate in Martian soil. [...] it does oxidize, and thus destroy, organics at the higher temperatures used in the Viking GCMS experiment. [...] The labeled release (LR) experiment (PI: Gilbert Levin, Biospherics Inc.) gave the most promise for exobiologists. In the LR experiment, a sample of Martian soil was inoculated with a drop of very dilute aqueous nutrient solution. The nutrients (7 molecular compounds that were Miller-Urey products) were tagged with radioactive 14C. [...] The result was quite a surprise, considering the negative results of the first two tests, with a steady stream of radioactive gases being given off by the soil immediately following the first injection. The experiment was done by both Viking probes, the first using a sample from the surface exposed to sunlight and the second probe taking the sample from underneath a rock; both initial injections came back positive. [...] Samples heated for 3 hours at 160 °C gave off no radioactive gas when nutrients were injected [...] A CNN article from 2000 noted that "Though most of his peers concluded otherwise, Levin still holds that the robot tests he coordinated on the 1976 Viking lander indicated the presence of living organisms on Mars." [...] on Mars, the second and third nutrient injections did not produce any further release of labeled gas." [...] ultraviolet light (remember: Mars lacks an ozone layer, so the surface is bathed in ultraviolet) can cause carbon dioxide to react with soils to produce various oxidizers, including highly reactive superoxides [...] Lastly, many superoxides are relatively unstable and are destroyed at elevated temperatures, also accounting for the "sterilization" seen in the LR experiment." [...] On 12 April 2012, an international team including Levin and Patricia Ann Straat published a peer reviewed paper suggesting the detection of "extant microbial life on Mars" [...] The general scientific community surmises that the Viking's biological tests remain inconclusive, and can be explained by purely chemical processes.

gancho: Em 2020, astrônomos anunciaram fosfina nas nuvens de Vênus, gás que na Terra se associa a seres vivos sem oxigênio. Reanálises acharam erros de calibração e o sinal encolheu ou sumiu. A briga segue aberta.
explicacao: A superfície de Vênus, perto de 462 °C e com pressão 92 vezes a da Terra, não permite vida como a conhecemos. Alguns cientistas especulam, porém, sobre micróbios nas camadas altas e ácidas das nuvens, onde a temperatura é amena. Por isso o anúncio de setembro de 2020 causou alvoroço: o radiotelescópio ALMA teria detectado fosfina, em cerca de 20 partes por bilhão, sem nenhum processo sem vida conhecido que a produzisse ali. A fosfina, além disso, não deveria durar muito naquela atmosfera. Logo vieram as contestações. Uma revisão do processamento dos dados achou erros de calibração que criavam linhas falsas; refeitas as contas, a fosfina sumia ou caía para 1 parte por bilhão, 20 vezes menos. Outra análise atribuiu o sinal ao dióxido de enxofre, e essa crítica também foi rebatida. Houve até uma nota publicada no site de uma comissão da União Astronômica Internacional acusando os autores de conduta antiética; a União disse não concordar com o texto, que foi retirado. Em 2022, o telescópio aerotransportado SOFIA não achou fosfina, mas uma reanálise dos mesmos dados viu cerca de 1 parte por bilhão. Em 2024, novas observações do programa JCMT-Venus voltaram a apoiar a detecção.

fontes.trecho: With extreme surface temperatures reaching nearly 735 K (462 °C; 863 °F) and an atmospheric pressure 92 times that of Earth, the conditions on Venus make water-based life as we know it impossible on the surface of the planet. However, a few scientists have speculated that thermoacidophilic extremophile microorganisms might exist in the temperate, acidic upper layers of the Venusian atmosphere. [...] Research published in September 2020 indicated the detection of phosphine (PH3) in Venus's atmosphere by Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) telescope that was not linked to any known abiotic method of production present or possible under Venusian conditions. However, the claimed detection of phosphine was disputed by several subsequent studies. A molecule like phosphine is not expected to persist in the Venusian atmosphere [...] PH3 is associated with anaerobic ecosystems on Earth, and may indicate life on anoxic planets. Related studies suggested that the initially claimed concentration of phosphine (20 ppb) [...] the authors of the September 2020 paper about phosphine were accused of unethical behaviour and criticized for being unscientific and misleading the public. [...] The statement was removed from the IAU website shortly thereafter. The IAU's media contact Lars Lindberg Christensen stated that IAU did not agree with the content of the letter [...] has revealed background calibration errors resulting in multiple spurious lines, including the spectral feature of phosphine. Re-analysis of data with a proper subtraction of background either does not result in the detection of the phosphine or detects it with concentration of 1ppb, 20 times below original estimate. [...] In 2022, observations of Venus using the SOFIA airborne infrared telescope failed to detect phosphine [...] A subsequent reanalysis of the SOFIA data using nonstandard calibration techniques resulted in a phosphine detection at the concentration level ~ 1 ppb [...] In 2024, the existence of phosphine on Venus was further corroborated with new observations by the JCMT-Venus programme. [...] the spectral line at 266.94 GHz attributed to phosphine in the clouds of Venus was more likely to have been produced by sulfur dioxide in the mesosphere. That claim was refuted in April 2021 for being inconsistent with the available data.

gancho: Em 1977, um radiotelescópio dos EUA captou por 72 segundos um sinal tão forte que o astrônomo escreveu "Wow!" ao lado dele na listagem. Nunca se repetiu. Em 2024, um estudo propôs uma causa natural rara.
explicacao: O sinal chegou em 15 de agosto de 1977 ao radiotelescópio Big Ear, da Universidade Estadual de Ohio, usado então na busca por inteligência extraterrestre. Dias depois, Jerry Ehman, que conferia à mão as folhas impressas pelo computador, circulou a sequência 6EQUJ5 e anotou "Wow!". A sequência não é uma mensagem: cada caractere indica a intensidade a cada intervalo, e o U indica cerca de 30 desvios-padrão acima do ruído de fundo. O telescópio era fixo e dependia da rotação da Terra para varrer o céu, então via cada ponto por só 72 segundos; um sinal vindo do espaço deveria crescer e diminuir nesse tempo, e foi o que aconteceu. A frequência estava perto dos 1420 MHz do hidrogênio, que Cocconi e Morrison tinham sugerido em 1959 como canal provável para civilizações se comunicarem. Um detalhe curioso: por um erro de digitação no pedido de compra, o oscilador do receptor veio 0,1 MHz acima do especificado, e o software teve de compensar. Buscas posteriores nunca reencontraram o sinal, e a ideia de que viesse de cometas foi rejeitada. Em 2024, uma equipe sugeriu que uma nuvem fria de hidrogênio, energizada por uma estrela, teria brilhado de repente.

fontes.trecho: The Wow! signal was a strong narrowband radio signal detected on August 15, 1977, by Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope in the United States, then used to support the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. [...] Astronomer Jerry R. Ehman discovered the anomaly a few days later while reviewing the recorded data. On the computer printout, he circled the reading of the signal's intensity, "6EQUJ5", and wrote the comment "Wow!" beside it [...] The entire signal sequence lasted for the full 72-second window during which Big Ear was able to observe it. Despite numerous follow-up searches and hypotheses [...] the signal has never recurred, and no explanation, terrestrial or otherwise, has been confirmed. [...] had speculated that any extraterrestrial civilization attempting to communicate via radio signals might do so using a frequency of 1420 megahertz (21-centimeter spectral line), which is naturally emitted by hydrogen [...] his job involved analyzing by hand large amounts of data processed by an IBM 1130 computer and recorded on line printer paper. [...] The string 6EQUJ5, commonly misinterpreted as a message encoded in the radio signal, represents in fact the signal's intensity variation over time [...] The Wow! signal's highest measured value was "U" (an intensity between 30 and 31), which is thirty standard deviations above background noise. [...] However, the university's purchasing department made a typographical error in the order form, instead obtaining an oscillator with frequency 1450.5056 MHz (i.e., 0.1 MHz higher than desired). The software used in the experiment was then written to adjust for this error. [...] relied on the rotation of the Earth to scan across the sky. Given the speed of Earth's rotation and the spatial width of the telescope's observation window, the Big Ear could observe any given point for just 72 seconds. [...] the recorded intensity of such a signal would display a gradual increase for the first 36 seconds—peaking at the center of the observation window—and then a gradual decrease as the telescope moved away from it. All these characteristics are present in the Wow! signal. [...] In August 2024, the Planetary Habitability Laboratory published a preprint reporting observations made in 2020 at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico, where they conclude that the Wow! signal was likely caused by a rare astrophysical event, in which stellar emissions energizing a cold hydrogen cloud caused it to suddenly surge in brightness. [...] This hypothesis was dismissed by astronomers, including members of the original Big Ear research team, as the cited comets were not in the beam at the correct time.
In September 1959, physicists Giuseppe Cocconi and Philip Morrison published an article in the journal Nature with the provocative title "Searching for Interstellar Communications".

gancho: A famosa equação de Drake, que estima quantas civilizações na galáxia poderiam se comunicar conosco, nasceu como pauta de uma reunião em 1961. Os dez participantes se apelidaram de "Ordem do Golfinho".
explicacao: Em 1960, o radioastrônomo Frank Drake fez a primeira busca sistemática por sinais de civilizações: escutou duas estrelas próximas parecidas com o Sol, de abril a julho, seis horas por dia, e não achou nada. Em 1961, organizou em Green Bank, nos EUA, a primeira reunião científica sobre o assunto. Dias antes, percebeu que precisava de uma pauta. Listou tudo o que seria preciso saber para prever a dificuldade de detectar vida extraterrestre e notou que, multiplicando os itens, saía um número: o de civilizações detectáveis na galáxia. Os fatores vão da taxa de formação de estrelas e da fração delas com planetas até a fração de planetas com vida, com inteligência e com tecnologia detectável, e o tempo durante o qual uma civilização emite sinais. Os palpites daquele encontro supunham que todo planeta adequado teria vida e que toda vida chegaria à inteligência. O resultado ia de 20 a 50 milhões de civilizações. Entre os dez presentes estavam Carl Sagan e o neurocientista John Lilly, que estudava a comunicação dos golfinhos, origem do apelido do grupo. A equação não foi feita para dar um número exato, e sim para organizar a discussão, e as incertezas dos fatores são tão grandes que ela não permite conclusões firmes.

fontes.trecho: The Drake equation is a probabilistic argument used to estimate the number of active, communicative extraterrestrial civilizations in the Milky Way Galaxy. The equation was formulated in 1961 by Frank Drake, not for purposes of quantifying the number of civilizations, but as a way to stimulate scientific dialogue at the first scientific meeting on the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI). [...] the uncertainty associated with any derived value is so large that the equation cannot be used to draw firm conclusions. [...] It was the first systematic search for signals from communicative extraterrestrial civilizations. [...] Drake monitored two nearby Sun-like stars: Epsilon Eridani and Tau Ceti, slowly scanning frequencies close to the 21 cm wavelength for six hours per day from April to July 1960. [...] It detected no signals. [...] The meeting was held at the Green Bank facility in 1961. The equation that bears Drake's name arose out of his preparations for the meeting. [...] As I planned the meeting, I realized a few day[s] ahead of time we needed an agenda. And so I wrote down all the things you needed to know to predict how hard it's going to be to detect extraterrestrial life. And looking at them it became pretty evident that if you multiplied all these together, you got a number, N, which is the number of detectable civilizations in our galaxy. [...] The ten attendees were conference organizer J. Peter Pearman, Frank Drake, Philip Morrison, businessman and radio amateur Dana Atchley, chemist Melvin Calvin, astronomer Su-Shu Huang, neuroscientist John C. Lilly, inventor Barney Oliver, astronomer Carl Sagan, and radio-astronomer Otto Struve. These participants called themselves "The Order of the Dolphin" (because of Lilly's work on dolphin communication) [...] fl = 1 (100% of these planets will develop life) fi = 1 (100% of which will develop intelligent life) [...] Inserting the above minimum numbers into the equation gives a minimum N of 20 (see: Range of results). Inserting the maximum numbers gives a maximum of 50,000,000.

gancho: O paradoxo de Fermi nasceu de uma pergunta solta num almoço em 1950: "Mas cadê todo mundo?". Os colegas riram, e todos entenderam na hora que ele falava de extraterrestres, embora o assunto já fosse outro.
explicacao: Em 1950, o físico Enrico Fermi visitava o laboratório de Los Alamos, nos EUA. A caminho do almoço, conversou com Emil Konopinski, Edward Teller e Herbert York sobre relatos de discos voadores e sobre a possibilidade de viajar mais rápido que a luz. O papo mudou de rumo, e Fermi disparou a pergunta, que cada um lembrou de um jeito: "Onde está todo mundo?", segundo Teller; "Mas cadê todo mundo?", segundo Konopinski. Teller contou que a mesa riu, e que todos entenderam de imediato que era sobre vida extraterrestre. As lembranças divergem sobre o que veio depois. York disse que Fermi fez uma série de contas, sobre planetas, vida, inteligência e a duração das civilizações, e concluiu que já deveríamos ter recebido visitas muitas vezes. Teller lembrou que ele só comentou que as distâncias talvez fossem enormes e que vivemos num canto afastado da galáxia. A pergunta apareceu impressa pela primeira vez numa nota de rodapé de um artigo de Carl Sagan, em 1963, e só num artigo de 1975 foi chamada de paradoxo. Versões da dúvida já apareciam em Fontenelle, Júlio Verne e Tsiolkovsky. Fermi nunca publicou nada sobre o tema, e Carl Sagan chegou a sugerir que a frase seria apócrifa. Para o pesquisador Robert Gray, a leitura tradicional distorce a pergunta: Fermi estaria duvidando da viabilidade da viagem interestelar, e não da existência de extraterrestres avançados.

fontes.trecho: The paradox is named after physicist Enrico Fermi who blurted out the question—remembered by Emil Konopinski as "But where is everybody?"—during lunchtime after the conversation had already moved on to other topics. This happened at Los Alamos in 1950 with colleagues Konopinski, Edward Teller, and Herbert York. The paradox first appeared in print in a 1963 paper by Carl Sagan [...] Early formulations of the paradox have also been identified in writings by Bernard Le Bovier de Fontenelle (1686) and Jules Verne (1865), and by Soviet rocket scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky (1933). [...] In 1950, Fermi visited Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico and, while walking to the Fuller Lodge for lunch, casually talked with fellow physicists Emil Konopinski, Edward Teller, and Herbert York about reports of flying saucers and the feasibility of faster-than-light travel. After the conversation had moved on to other topics, Fermi blurted out his question which has been variously recalled as: "Where is everybody?" (Teller), "Don't you ever wonder where everybody is?" (York), or "But where is everybody?" (Konopinski). According to Teller, "The result of his question was general laughter because of the strange fact that, in spite of Fermi's question coming out of the blue, everybody around the table seemed to understand at once that he was talking about extraterrestrial life." [...] According to York, Fermi "followed up with a series of calculations on the probability of earthlike planets, the probability of life given an earth, the probability of humans given life, the likely rise and duration of high technology, and so on. He concluded on the basis of such calculations that we ought to have been visited long ago and many times over." However, Teller recalled that Fermi did not elaborate on his question beyond "perhaps a statement that the distances to the next location of living beings may be very great and that, indeed, as far as our galaxy is concerned, we are living somewhere in the sticks, far removed from the metropolitan area of the galactic center." [...] The Fermi question first appeared in print in a footnote of a 1963 paper by Carl Sagan. [...] and a 1975 article in JBIS Interstellar Studies by David Viewing that first described it as a paradox. [...] Fermi did not publish anything regarding the paradox, with Sagan once suggesting the quote to be apocryphal. [...] According to Gray, the current understanding of the paradox misinterprets Fermi's question and subsequent discussion, which was challenging the feasibility of interstellar travel rather than the existence of advanced extraterrestrial life. [...] Scientists like Robert Gray have criticized its attribution to Fermi

gancho: Conta-se que bactérias da Terra sobreviveram dois anos e meio na Lua, numa câmera que a Apollo 12 trouxe de volta. A história é contestada: a contaminação pode ter ocorrido depois, já na Terra.
explicacao: A sonda americana Surveyor 3 pousou na Lua em abril de 1967. Em novembro de 1969, os astronautas Pete Conrad e Alan Bean, da Apollo 12, pousaram a uma distância que dava para ir a pé, examinaram a sonda e trouxeram para a Terra cerca de 10 kg de peças, entre elas a câmera de TV. Até hoje, é a única sonda visitada por humanos em outro mundo. A câmera tinha passado 947 dias no vácuo, incluindo noites lunares abaixo de −130 °C. Daí nasceu uma história muito repetida: a bactéria Streptococcus mitis, uma bactéria comum, teria contaminado a câmera antes do lançamento e sobrevivido dormente na Lua até ser achada no laboratório. O caso foi citado como apoio à ideia de que a vida pode viajar entre planetas. Pesquisadores independentes, porém, contestam a conclusão: a contaminação pode ter vindo de um recipiente que não vedava bem ou da coleta de amostras na sala limpa, depois da volta da Apollo 12. Com ou sem micróbios na Lua, o episódio é lembrado no contexto das regras rígidas que a NASA adotou para não levar vida da Terra a Marte e a outros mundos.

fontes.trecho: Surveyor 3 was visited by Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean in November 1969, and remains the only probe visited by humans on another world. The Apollo 12 astronauts excised several components of Surveyor 3, including the television camera, and returned them to Earth for study. [...] Launched on April 17, 1967, Surveyor 3 landed on April 20, 1967 [...] Landing within walking distance on November 19, 1969 [...] they brought back about 22 pounds (10 kg) of parts of the Surveyor to the Earth, including its TV camera [...] Analysis of the camera found that it withstood 947 days in the vacuum of space, including 32 two-week lunar nights with temperatures dropping below −200 °F (−130 °C) [...] It is widely claimed that a common type of bacterium, Streptococcus mitis, accidentally contaminated the Surveyor's camera prior to launch, and that the bacteria survived dormant in the harsh lunar environment for two and a half years, supposedly then to be detected when Apollo 12 brought the Surveyor's camera back to the Earth. This claim has been cited by some as providing credence to the idea of interplanetary panspermia, but more importantly, it led NASA to adopt strict abiotic procedures for space probes to prevent contamination of the planet Mars and other astronomical bodies [...] However, independent investigators have challenged the claim of surviving bacteria on Surveyor 3 on the Moon. There is a possibility the contamination was caused by using a non-airtight container, or when the samples  were being taken in the clean room after Apollo 12.

gancho: No fim das missões, a NASA jogou de propósito a sonda Galileo em Júpiter, em 2003, e a Cassini em Saturno, em 2017. O motivo: evitar que micróbios terrestres a bordo caíssem por acidente em luas que podem ter vida.
explicacao: A preocupação tem nome: contaminação direta, a transferência de organismos vivos da Terra para outro corpo celeste. Se micróbios clandestinos chegassem a um oceano como o de Europa, lua de Júpiter, ou o de Encélado, lua de Saturno, poderiam atrapalhar para sempre a busca por vida nativa. A Galileo, que estudou Júpiter e suas luas, não tinha mais combustível para escapar da gravidade do planeta. Em 21 de setembro de 2003, foi lançada contra a atmosfera de Júpiter, justamente para não contaminar Europa. A Cassini teve um fim mais elaborado, o "Grande Final": 22 órbitas arriscadas pelo vão entre Saturno e seus anéis internos, colhendo dados inéditos, antes do mergulho na atmosfera do planeta em 15 de setembro de 2017. A destruição foi escolhida para que a sonda, já sem energia ou sem comunicação, não acabasse batendo numa lua possivelmente habitável. O governo americano aprovou o Grande Final ao custo de 200 milhões de dólares. O último sinal chegou 30 segundos depois do previsto, e estima-se que a nave tenha se desfeito cerca de 45 segundos após a última transmissão.

fontes.trecho: Galileo was intentionally destroyed in Jupiter's atmosphere on September 21, 2003 to prevent it from contaminating any of Jupiter's moons. [...] Lacking the fuel to escape Jupiter's gravity well, at the end of Galileo's life, the main spacecraft was deliberately crashed into Jupiter on September 21, 2003, to prevent forward contamination of possible life of Jupiter's moon Europa.

The mission ended on September 15, 2017, when Cassini's trajectory took it into Saturn's upper atmosphere and it burned up in order to prevent any risk of contaminating Saturn's moons, which might have offered habitable environments to stowaway terrestrial microbes on the spacecraft. [...] At the end of its mission, the Cassini spacecraft executed its "Grand Finale": a number of risky passes through the gaps between Saturn and its inner rings. [...] the spacecraft was intentionally destroyed to prevent potential contamination of Saturn's moons if Cassini were to unintentionally crash into them when maneuvering the probe was no longer possible due to power loss or other communication issues at the end of its operational lifespan. [...] The U.S. government in late 2014 approved the Grand Finale at the cost of $200 million. [...] After a further 22 orbits through the gap, the mission was ended with a dive into Saturn's atmosphere on September 15; signal was lost at 11:55:46 UTC  on September 15, 2017, 30 seconds later than predicted. It is estimated that the spacecraft burned up about 45 seconds after the last transmission.
Forward contamination is the transfer of viable organisms from Earth to another celestial body.

gancho: Em 2019, uma sonda israelense se espatifou na Lua levando tardígrados desidratados, postos a bordo na última hora. Cogitou-se que sobreviveram; um estudo de 2021 concluiu que a batida muito provavelmente os matou.
explicacao: A Beresheet, da organização SpaceIL e da Israel Aerospace Industries, era uma pequena sonda de demonstração. Levava uma "cápsula do tempo" com mais de 30 milhões de páginas de dados, entre elas uma cópia completa da Wikipedia em inglês. Na última hora, amostras genéticas e tardígrados, animais microscópicos que em missões anteriores já tinham sobrevivido algum tempo ao vácuo do espaço, foram incluídos em resina entre as camadas digitais. Em 11 de abril de 2019, um giroscópio falhou durante a frenagem e o motor principal se desligou. Quando voltou, era tarde: a 150 metros de altura, a nave ainda passava de 500 km/h, e se perdeu no impacto. Em agosto de 2019, cientistas disseram que os tardígrados, em estado de vida suspensa, talvez tivessem sobrevivido. O episódio rendeu críticas pela falta de medidas de proteção planetária e de regras internacionais que as imponham. Em maio de 2021, uma equipe liderada por Alejandra Traspas, estudante da Universidade Queen Mary de Londres, afirmou que eles muito provavelmente foram destruídos pela força da queda.

fontes.trecho: was a demonstrator of a small robotic lunar lander and lunar probe operated by SpaceIL and Israel Aerospace Industries. [...] The lander's gyroscopes failed on 11 April 2019 causing the main engine to shut off, which resulted in the lander crashing on the Moon. [...] The spacecraft carried a "time capsule" containing over 30 million pages of data, including a full copy of the English-language Wikipedia [...] At the last minute, genetic samples and tardigrades were added in epoxy resin between the digital layers. [...] On previous space missions, tardigrades were exposed to the open vacuum of space and some were able to live for a period of time. [...] An Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU2) gyroscope failed during the braking procedure on approach to the landing site [...] The final telemetry reading indicated that at an altitude of 150 m (490 ft) the craft was still traveling at over 500 km/h (310 mph; 140 m/s), resulting in a total loss on impact with the lunar surface. [...] In August 2019, scientists reported that a capsule containing tardigrade micro-animals in their natural cryptobiotic state may have survived the crash and lived on the Moon for a while. [...] this "tardigrade affair" attracted the criticism of professionals who pointed out the lack of both planetary protection measures and international regulation to enforce such measures. In May 2021, a team of researchers led by Alejandra Traspas, a student at Queen Mary University of London, claimed that the tardigrades were most likely destroyed by the force of the crash.

gancho: O fósforo, o mais escasso dos elementos essenciais à vida, nunca tinha sido achado num oceano fora da Terra. Em 2023, grãos de gelo de Encélado indicaram que o oceano dessa lua tem ao menos 100 vezes mais que os nossos.
explicacao: Encélado, lua de Saturno, esconde um oceano global sob uma crosta de gelo, e gêiseres no polo sul lançam esse material ao espaço. A sonda Cassini atravessou as plumas e analisou o que saía delas. Em 2017, a NASA anunciou que um espectrômetro de massa tinha detectado ali hidrogênio molecular, provavelmente vindo de atividade hidrotermal no fundo do oceano. Esse hidrogênio é comida em potencial: na Terra, micróbios chamados metanogênicos o combinam com gás carbônico e produzem metano. Faltava o fósforo, cosmicamente o menos abundante dos elementos de que a vida precisa. Modelos chegaram a sugerir que ele seria raro em oceanos de luas geladas. Em 2023, uma análise de grãos de gelo registrados pelo analisador de poeira da Cassini achou fosfatos de sódio. Somada a experimentos de laboratório, ela indica concentração de fósforo pelo menos 100 vezes maior que a média dos oceanos da Terra. Com isso, Encélado passa a ter o conjunto básico de ingredientes químicos da vida: carbono, hidrogênio, nitrogênio, oxigênio, enxofre e fósforo. Segundo os autores, é muito improvável que o fósforo limite uma possível vida ali. Ninguém achou vida, mas o ambiente parece cada vez mais habitável.

fontes.titulo: Detection of phosphates originating from Enceladus's ocean (Postberg et al., Nature, 2023)
fontes.trecho: Phosphorus, the least abundant of the bio-essential elements [...] has not yet been detected in an ocean beyond Earth. Earlier geochemical modelling studies suggest that phosphate might be scarce in the ocean of Enceladus and other icy ocean worlds [...] Here we present Cassini’s Cosmic Dust Analyzer mass spectra of ice grains emitted by Enceladus that show the presence of sodium phosphates. Our observational results, together with laboratory analogue experiments, suggest that phosphorus is readily available in Enceladus’s ocean in the form of orthophosphates, with phosphorus concentrations at least 100-fold higher in the moon’s plume-forming ocean waters than in Earth’s oceans. [...] phosphorus is cosmochemically the least abundant and has not previously been detected at any of the ocean-bearing moons in the Solar System. [...] which is thus extremely unlikely to be a limiting factor in the survival of putative life on Enceladus

Cryovolcanoes near the south pole shoot geyser-like jets of water vapour, molecular hydrogen, other volatiles, and solid material [...] In June 2023, astronomers reported that various phosphates had been detected on Enceladus, completing the set of basic chemical ingredients for life there (carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur and phosporus). [...] On April 13, 2017, NASA announced the discovery of possible hydrothermal activity on Enceladus's sub-surface ocean floor. [...] A mass spectrometer on the craft detected molecular hydrogen (H2) from the plume, and after months of analysis, the conclusion was made that the hydrogen was most likely the result of hydrothermal activity beneath the surface. [...] could use it to obtain energy by combining the hydrogen with carbon dioxide dissolved in the water. The chemical reaction is known as "methanogenesis" because it produces methane as a byproduct [...] suggests that the entire icy crust is detached from the rocky core and therefore that a global ocean is present beneath the surface

gancho: A superfície gelada de Europa, lua de Júpiter, produz cerca de mil toneladas de oxigênio por dia, sem precisar de seres vivos: partículas carregadas, levadas pelo campo magnético de Júpiter, quebram a água do gelo.
explicacao: Europa fica no meio dos cinturões de radiação de Júpiter. Partículas eletricamente carregadas, arrastadas pelo enorme campo magnético do planeta, bombardeiam o gelo da superfície e partem moléculas de água em hidrogênio e oxigênio. O hidrogênio, mais leve, escapa; o oxigênio forma uma atmosfera finíssima. Em 29 de setembro de 2022, a sonda Juno passou a 354 km de Europa, e um de seus instrumentos mediu os íons de hidrogênio e oxigênio arrancados da lua. Com isso, a equipe calculou a produção de oxigênio em cerca de 12 kg por segundo, ou mil toneladas a cada 24 horas: o bastante para um milhão de pessoas respirarem por um dia. Parece muito, mas é bem menos que a maioria das estimativas anteriores, que iam de poucos quilos a mais de mil quilos por segundo. O interesse vai além do número. Europa tem, sob o gelo, um oceano de água salgada, e os cientistas acreditam que parte desse oxigênio possa migrar até ele e servir de fonte de energia para metabolismo. Quanto dele chega lá ainda é uma pergunta que a sonda Europa Clipper, com chegada prevista a Júpiter em 2030, vai investigar.

fontes.titulo: NASA's Juno Mission Measures Oxygen Production at Europa (NASA, 2024)
fontes.trecho: The ice-covered Jovian moon generates 1,000 tons of oxygen every 24 hours – enough to keep a million humans breathing for a day. [...] Scientists with NASA’s Juno mission to Jupiter have calculated the rate of oxygen being produced at the Jovian moon Europa to be substantially less than most previous studies. [...] The paper’s authors estimate the amount of oxygen produced to be around 26 pounds every second (12 kilograms per second). Previous estimates range from a few pounds to over 2,000 pounds per second (over 1,000 kilograms per second). Scientists believe that some of the oxygen produced in this manner could work its way into the moon’s subsurface ocean as a possible source of metabolic energy. [...] Scientists believe a vast internal ocean of salty water lurks beneath its icy crust [...] Europa’s orbit places it right in the middle of the gas giant’s radiation belts. Charged, or ionized, particles from Jupiter bombard the icy surface, splitting water molecules in two to generate oxygen that might find its way into the moon’s ocean. [...] the stream is a fluid of ionized particles swept around Jupiter by its extraordinary magnetic field [...] As Juno flew within 220 miles (354 kilometers) of Europa at 2:36 p.m. PDT Sept. 29, 2022, JADE identified and measured hydrogen and oxygen ions that had been created by the bombarding charged particles [...] Oxygen production is one of many facets that NASA’s Europa Clipper mission will investigate when it arrives at Jupiter in 2030.
As it continues to move, the hydrogen is light enough to pass through the surface gravity of the atmosphere leaving behind only oxygen.

gancho: Em 2005, previu-se que, se houvesse vida em Titã consumindo hidrogênio, o gás rarearia perto da superfície. Em 2010, dados sugeriram isso. É só hipótese: o autor da previsão achou outras causas mais prováveis.
explicacao: Titã, lua de Saturno, tem rios e lagos de metano e etano líquidos. Especula-se que, ali, possa existir vida usando esses líquidos como os seres da Terra usam a água. Esses organismos hipotéticos absorveriam hidrogênio no lugar de oxigênio, reagiriam com acetileno no lugar de glicose e soltariam metano no lugar de gás carbônico, algo parecido com o que fazem micróbios metanogênicos na Terra. Em 2005, Christopher McKay e Heather Smith previram o efeito disso na atmosfera: menos acetileno que o esperado e menos hidrogênio perto do chão. Em junho de 2010, Darrell Strobel, da Universidade Johns Hopkins, mostrou que há muito mais hidrogênio no alto da atmosfera do que perto da superfície, o que obriga o gás a descer, e que perto do chão ele parece desaparecer. No mesmo mês, outro estudo achou níveis muito baixos de acetileno na superfície. McKay concordou que vida era uma explicação possível, mas alertou que outras eram mais prováveis: erro humano, algum processo meteorológico ou um mineral que faça hidrogênio e acetileno reagirem a −178 °C. Esse catalisador é desconhecido e seria, ele mesmo, uma descoberta espantosa. A missão Dragonfly vai medir, entre outras coisas, o hidrogênio perto da superfície.

fontes.trecho: It has been speculated that life could exist in the liquid methane and ethane that form rivers and lakes on Titan's surface, just as organisms on Earth live in water. Such hypothetical creatures would take in H2 in place of O2, react it with acetylene instead of glucose, and produce methane instead of carbon dioxide. By comparison, some methanogens on Earth obtain energy by reacting hydrogen with carbon dioxide, producing methane and water. In 2005, astrobiologists Christopher McKay and Heather Smith predicted that if methanogenic life is consuming atmospheric hydrogen in sufficient volume, it will have a measurable effect on the mixing ratio in the troposphere of Titan. The effects predicted included a level of acetylene much lower than otherwise expected, as well as a reduction in the concentration of hydrogen itself. Evidence consistent with these predictions was reported in June 2010 by Darrell Strobel of Johns Hopkins University, who analysed measurements of hydrogen concentration in the upper and lower atmosphere. Strobel found that the hydrogen concentration in the upper atmosphere is so much larger than near the surface that the physics of diffusion leads to hydrogen flowing downwards [...] Near the surface the downward-flowing hydrogen apparently disappears. Another paper released the same month showed very low levels of acetylene on Titan's surface. Chris McKay agreed with Strobel that presence of life, as suggested in McKay's 2005 article, is a possible explanation for the findings about hydrogen and acetylene, but also cautioned that other explanations are currently more likely: namely the possibility that the results are due to human error, to a meteorological process, or to the presence of some mineral catalyst enabling hydrogen and acetylene to react chemically. He noted that such a catalyst, one effective at −178 °C (95 K), is presently unknown and would in itself be a startling discovery, though less startling than discovery of an extraterrestrial life form. [...] to sample the lower atmosphere for possible biosignatures, including hydrogen concentrations.

gancho: O metano, que pode indicar vida microbiana, já foi "detectado" em Marte várias vezes. O jipe Curiosity viu picos; um orbitador europeu, nada. Em 2025, surgiu uma suspeita: vazamento de metano terrestre no instrumento.
explicacao: A história começa em 1969, quando a equipe da sonda Mariner 7 anunciou metano e amônia perto do polo de Marte. O anúncio foi retirado: o sinal vinha de gelo de gás carbônico. Desde então, telescópios na Terra, orbitadores e jipes relataram valores que vão de 60 partes por bilhão até abaixo do limite de detecção, e não há consenso de que o gás exista mesmo lá. Em 2013 e 2014, o Curiosity mediu na cratera Gale uma alta de menos de 1 para cerca de 7 partes por bilhão, que depois voltou ao normal. Já o orbitador europeu ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, desde 2019, não acha metano, com limites cada vez mais baixos. Uma ideia para conciliar os dois é que o metano se acumule à noite perto do chão e se dilua de dia, quando o orbitador mede. Há outro nó: pelos modelos, o metano duraria séculos na atmosfera marciana; para que picos apareçam e sumam, ele teria de ser destruído pelo menos 600 vezes mais rápido, por um mecanismo desconhecido. As fontes possíveis incluem reações entre água e rocha e, em tese, micróbios metanogênicos, de que não há nenhuma evidência. Em 2025, foi apresentada a possibilidade de vazamentos de metano terrestre dentro do próprio espectrômetro do Curiosity.

fontes.trecho: The potential presence of methane in the atmosphere of Mars may indicate the presence of microbial life or geological activity. [...] Measurements of methane from 60 ppbv to under the detection limit (<0.05 ppbv) have been reported, but there is no scientific consensus on whether these observations genuinely corroborate the existence of methane on Mars. [...] In 1969, the Mariner 7 science team reported in a press conference that methane and ammonia had been detected near the Marian polar ice cap. However, that claim was retracted after subsequent analyses revealed that the spectrometric signals were actually produced by carbon dioxide ice. [...] A rise from <1 to 7±2 ppbv was observed from 2013 to 2014, followed by a drop back down to baseline levels, suggesting that Gale Crater may be episodically releasing methane from an unknown source. [...] In 2025, the possibility of leaks of terrestrial methane in the foreoptics chamber of the Tunable Laser Spectrometer was presented as a potential explanation for previous methane measurements by the rover. [...] In 2019, the Trace Gas Orbiter on ExoMars reported non-detections of methane in Mars's upper atmosphere (5 km altitude), with an upper limit of 50 pptv. The ExoMars non-detections contradict the methane detections in Gale crater by the Curiosity rover. [...] ExoMars measurements occur in the daytime and report non-detections. Should there be high concentrations of methane at night, higher surface temperatures during the day could cause convection currents that mix and dilute methane with the bulk atmosphere. Extensive further search of methane by ExoMars reported non-detections, with upper limits of 0.02 ppbv. [...] The principal candidates for the origin of Mars's methane include non-biological processes such as water-rock reactions [...] However, there is no evidence for the presence of such organisms on Mars. [...] current photochemical models suggest that the atmospheric lifetime of methane on Mars is several centuries, which is contradictory to reports of methane plumes and seasonal or diurnal cycles. To reconcile reported methane detections with current knowledge of photochemistry, methane degradation would need to be at least 600 times faster than previously expected based on atmosphere composition, necessitating the existence of an as-yet-unknown methane destruction mechanism.

gancho: Por medo de micróbios lunares, os astronautas da Apollo 11 passaram 21 dias em quarentena. Pelos próprios critérios de projeto, o sistema falhou: o material da Lua escapou da contenção no mar e no laboratório.
explicacao: A chance de trazer germes da Lua era considerada remota, mas a NASA não quis arriscar, e milhares de americanos lhe escreveram cartas preocupados com uma possível praga. Ao pousar no oceano, em 1969, os astronautas vestiram roupas de isolamento biológico ainda no mar, foram esfregados com solução de hipoclorito de sódio, e o bote usado na descontaminação foi afundado de propósito. No porta-aviões, entraram num trailer de quarentena e depois seguiram para o Laboratório de Recepção Lunar, que também guardava as rochas trazidas. As regras, reunidas na chamada Lei de Exposição Extraterrestre, foram divulgadas em 16 de julho de 1969, dia do lançamento, o que evitou o debate público. Em 10 de agosto, a quarentena foi suspensa. O procedimento se repetiu nas Apollo 12 e 14 e foi abandonado a partir da Apollo 15. Revisões posteriores foram duras: os métodos seriam inadequados pelos padrões atuais, e o laboratório seria considerado um fracasso pelos próprios critérios, porque o material lunar não ficou contido, com dois pontos de falha na volta da Apollo 11, na amerissagem e no próprio prédio. Até hoje, é a única tentativa de trazer amostras que, na época, poderiam conter vida extraterrestre.

fontes.trecho: Saturn V AS-506 launched Apollo 11 on July 16, 1969 [...] The divers then passed biological isolation garments (BIGs) to the astronauts, and assisted them into the life raft. The possibility of bringing back pathogens from the lunar surface was considered remote, but NASA took precautions at the recovery site. The astronauts were rubbed down with a sodium hypochlorite solution [...] The raft containing decontamination materials was intentionally sunk. [...] where they would begin the Earth-based portion of their 21 days of quarantine. This practice would continue for two more Apollo missions, Apollo 12 and Apollo 14, before the Moon was proven to be barren of life, and the quarantine process dropped. [...] In accordance with the Extra-Terrestrial Exposure Law, a set of regulations promulgated by NASA on July 16 to codify its quarantine protocol [...] After three weeks in confinement (first in the Apollo spacecraft, then in their trailer on Hornet, and finally in the Lunar Receiving Laboratory), the astronauts were given a clean bill of health. On August 10, 1969, the Interagency Committee on Back Contamination met in Atlanta and lifted the quarantine on the astronauts

The Lunar Receiving Laboratory (LRL) was a facility at NASA's Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center (Building 37) that was constructed to quarantine astronauts and material brought back from the Moon during the Apollo program to reduce the risk of back-contamination. [...] After recovery at sea, crews from Apollo 11, Apollo 12, and  Apollo 14 walked from their helicopter to the Mobile Quarantine Facility on the deck of an aircraft carrier and were brought to the LRL for quarantine. [...] The quarantine requirement was dropped for Apollo 15 and later missions.

The Apollo era quarantine procedures are of interest as the only attempt to date of a return to Earth of a sample that, at the time, was thought to have a remote possibility of including extraterrestrial life. Samples and astronauts were quarantined in the Lunar Receiving Laboratory. The methods used would be considered inadequate for containment by modern standards. Also the lunar receiving laboratory would be judged a failure by its own design criteria as the sample return didn't contain the lunar material, with two failure points during the Apollo 11 return mission, at the splashdown and at the facility itself.

The Apollo missions incited public concern about the possibility of microbes on the Moon, creating fears about a plague being brought to Earth when the astronauts returned. NASA received thousands of letters from Americans concerned with the potential for back contamination. [...] In the Apollo era, NASA delayed announcement of its quarantine regulations until the day Apollo was launched, bypassing the requirement for public debate

gancho: Em 1990, Carl Sagan convenceu a NASA a apontar a sonda Galileo, de passagem, para a Terra, como se buscasse vida num planeta desconhecido. Ela achou oxigênio, metano fora de equilíbrio e rádio de origem "inteligente".
explicacao: A passagem foi consequência de uma tragédia. Depois da explosão do ônibus espacial Challenger, em 1986, a NASA desistiu de mandar a Galileo direto para Júpiter e a fez dar voltas por Vênus e pela Terra para ganhar impulso gravitacional. Em 8 de dezembro de 1990, a sonda passaria a 960 km da superfície terrestre. Sagan convenceu a agência a usar os instrumentos para fazer um teste: daria para reconhecer vida na Terra vista de fora? A regra era tratar a vida como a hipótese de último recurso. Fotos da Austrália e da Antártida não mostraram sinais de civilização. Mas a sonda mediu oxigênio e metano em proporções que indicavam um desequilíbrio químico causado por seres vivos, viu no infravermelho a "borda vermelha" típica da vegetação e captou transmissões de rádio com jeito de coisa fabricada. Com humor, a equipe escreveu que havia bons argumentos para atribuí-las a uma forma de vida inteligente. O artigo, publicado na Nature em 1993, não foi fácil de aprovar, porque não descrevia nada de novo. Virou um experimento de controle que serve até hoje de modelo para buscar sinais de vida em exoplanetas.

fontes.titulo: How Would We Know There's Life on Earth? This Bold Experiment Found Out (Scientific American / Nature, 2023)
fontes.trecho: Almost four years before Galileo’s launch, in January 1986, the space shuttle Challenger had exploded shortly after lift-off, taking seven lives with it. NASA cancelled its plans to dispatch Galileo on a speedy path to Jupiter using a liquid-fuelled rocket aboard another space shuttle. [...] with mission engineers slingshotting it around Venus and Earth so it could gain the gravitational boosts that would catapult it all the way to Jupiter. On 8 December 1990, Galileo was due to skim past Earth, just 960 kilometres above the surface. [...] He talked NASA into pointing the spacecraft’s instruments at our planet. The resulting paper was titled ‘A search for life on Earth from the Galileo spacecraft.’ [...] The existence of life was to be, in the words of the paper, the “hypothesis of last resort” for explaining what Galileo observed. [...] High-resolution images of Australia and Antarctica obtained as Galileo flew overhead did not yield signs of civilization. Still, Galileo measured oxygen and methane in Earth’s atmosphere, the latter in ratios that suggested a disequilibrium brought about by living organisms. It spotted a steep cliff in the infrared spectrum of sunlight reflecting off the planet, a distinctive ‘red edge’ that indicates the presence of vegetation. And it picked up radio transmissions coming from the surface that were moderated as if engineered. “A strong case can be made that the signals are generated by an intelligent form of life on Earth,” Sagan’s team wrote, rather cheekily. [...] Editorial approval for the paper was far from unanimous, because it was not obviously describing something new. [...] “It was an incredibly powerful control experiment for something that wasn’t really on many people’s radar at the time,” he says. [...] When Sagan and his colleagues pointed Galileo at Earth, they invented a scientific framework for looking for signs of life on these other worlds — one that has permeated every search for such biosignatures since.

fontes.titulo: Beyond the Galileo Experiment (NASA Astrobiology Institute, 2019)
fontes.trecho: Nearly 30 years after its publication, A search for life on Earth from the Galileo spacecraft by Sagan et al. (1993) establishes a foundation for the present and future of biosignature detection in our Solar System and beyond.

gancho: A hipótese de Gaia nasceu de um trabalho para a NASA: James Lovelock concluiu que Marte não tinha vida só de olhar sua atmosfera, quimicamente estável, tão diferente da mistura química agitada da biosfera terrestre.
explicacao: Em 1961, a NASA contratou o cientista inglês James Lovelock para desenvolver instrumentos sensíveis capazes de analisar atmosferas e superfícies de outros planetas. Trabalhando num precursor do programa Viking, ele raciocinou que seres vivos em Marte teriam de usar a atmosfera do planeta e, com isso, alterá-la. Mas a atmosfera marciana estava em estado estável, perto do equilíbrio químico: muito gás carbônico e quase nada de oxigênio, metano ou hidrogênio. Para Lovelock, o contraste com a mistura quimicamente dinâmica da Terra indicava com força que Marte não tinha vida. As sondas Viking procuraram assim mesmo, sem sucesso. Dessa linha de trabalho, e de pesquisas para a petroleira Shell, saiu nos anos 1960 a hipótese de Gaia: a ideia de que as partes vivas e não vivas da Terra formam um sistema complexo que se autorregula, como se fosse um único organismo. O nome, da deusa grega da Terra, foi sugestão do romancista William Golding. Lovelock, que morreu em 2022, no dia do próprio aniversário, também inventou o detector de captura de elétrons, com o qual foi o primeiro a detectar a presença generalizada de CFCs na atmosfera.

fontes.trecho: James Ephraim Lovelock (26 July 1919 – 26 July 2022) was an English independent scientist, environmentalist and futurist. He is best known for proposing the Gaia hypothesis, which postulates that the Earth functions as a self-regulating system. [...] He invented the electron capture detector and, using it, became the first to detect the widespread presence of chlorofluorocarbons in the atmosphere. [...] In early 1961, Lovelock was engaged by NASA to develop sensitive instruments for the analysis of extraterrestrial atmospheres and planetary surfaces. [...] During work on a precursor of this program, Lovelock became interested in the composition of the Martian atmosphere, reasoning that many life forms on Mars would be obliged to make use of it (and, thus, alter it). However, the atmosphere was found to be in a stable condition close to its chemical equilibrium, with very little oxygen, methane, or hydrogen, but with an overwhelming abundance of carbon dioxide. To Lovelock, the stark contrast between the Martian atmosphere and chemically dynamic mixture of the Earth's biosphere was strongly indicative of the absence of life on Mars. However, when they were finally launched to Mars, the Viking probes still searched (unsuccessfully) for extant life there. [...] Lovelock first formulated the Gaia hypothesis in the 1960s resulting from his work for NASA concerned with detecting life on Mars and his work with Royal Dutch Shell. The hypothesis proposes that living and non-living parts of the Earth form a complex interacting system that can be thought of as a single organism. Named after the Greek goddess Gaia at the suggestion of novelist William Golding
